articles.html:
The wiki replaced the loose SOP binders in March 2005. The binder pages were typed in as they stood, and they have been edited since by the people who use them. The paper binders were kept and are reprinted from the wiki.

Who edits

  • Anyone with an OER account can edit any page.
  • Pages in WATCH FLOOR are owned by the Watch Leads. Change the wording if you like; a change to what someone must do needs a Lead's name in the edit summary.
  • Pages in ENGINEERING are owned by the engineer for that system. The owner is named at the top of the page where it matters.
  • Pages in ESCALATION and PHYSICAL SECURITY change only with the security engineer or the Technical Lead named in the summary. When one changes, the binder copy is reprinted the same day.

How to write a page

  • Say what to do first, then why.
  • Write steps as numbered lists. One action per step.
  • Use the names people use on the floor: COMM, not "communications position".
  • Times are facility local time unless the page says UTC.
  • Link to the drawing in the Document Register rather than copying it.
  • Every edit needs a summary. "Fixed" is not a summary.

What never goes in the wiki

  • Passwords, PINs, safe combinations or door codes. They are held in the sealed envelopes in the security office safe.
  • Home phone numbers or addresses. The Emergency Call-Out uses the sealed contact file.
  • Anything about a person's leave reasons, health or reviews.
WARNING: A wiki page is not the procedure in force until the binder copy is reprinted. During a wiki outage, or if the page and the binder disagree, follow the binder and tell the Lead.

articles.title: Escalation Paths: Overview
articles.summary: The four ladders (watch, engineering, security, facilities), the 10-minute rule and when to skip a rung.

revs.s: One page for all escalation, from the four binder sheets.
Watch ladder checked against the floor.
OPS DUTY replaces calling the senior Lead at home.
Shared-cause rule after the 11 February feed outage.
A NOMINAL tile is not proof that data is arriving.

articles.html:
Escalation means telling the next person up who can decide or act. You never need permission to escalate. Escalating something that turns out to be nothing is not a mistake; sitting on something is.

The four ladders

LadderFirst callThenThenPage
WatchLead (in the room)OPS DUTY, ext 4011Technical LeadEscalation: Watch Floor
EngineeringDuty engineer, ext 4030System ownerTechnical LeadEscalation: Engineering
SecurityGuard desk, ext 4020Security engineerPolice (guard desk calls)Escalation: Security
FacilitiesFacilities desk, ext 4040 (guard desk after hours)Contractor on the cardInfrastructure engineerEscalation: Facilities and Contractors

The 10-minute rule

  1. Call the first name on the ladder.
  2. If there is no answer in 10 minutes, call the next rung. Do not wait for a call back.
  3. Log each call in the watch log or maintenance log with the time, who you called and whether they answered.
  4. When someone takes it, they own it until they hand it back. Say so on the call: "You have it."

Skip a rung when

  • People are in danger: outside emergency services first, then the guard desk. See Evacuation and Shelter.
  • Two or more monitors go DEGRADED or DATA SUSPECT within 15 minutes of each other. Treat it as one shared cause and page the duty engineer at once, even if each source looks fine on its own. (11 February 2026: three feeds behind one content network nobody had listed.)
  • Any CRITICAL contact or a CRITICAL overall status: the Lead calls OPS DUTY and the duty engineer together.
  • The watch floor cannot keep three seats filled. Call OPS DUTY at once.
  • A door forced alarm on zone 3 or zone 4. Guard desk and security engineer together.

What a NOMINAL tile does not mean

NOTE: From 8 July 2026 the tiles compare the newest record time with each source's own interval and show DATA SUSPECT when the data is old. Before that, a tile could read NOMINAL with a current check time while nothing new had arrived for hours (7 July 2026, five sources). If anything on the floor looks too quiet, check LAST GOOD DATA before you believe the tile. See Troubleshooting: Feed Silent or Data Old.

After any escalation

  • The person who took it writes the closing entry: what happened, what was done, what is still open.
  • Open items go on the turnover sheet. See Shift Turnover.
  • If this page or a ladder was wrong, fix it the same day and reprint the binder page.

From a seat to the Lead

Tell the Lead out loud, at the Lead position, for anything you are not sure about. The Lead decides whether it goes further. If the Lead is off the floor, tell the next senior seat (COMM, then Correlation) and send someone for the Lead.

  • Monitoring: any tile that changes level, any contact at ELEVATED or above, any source DEGRADED.
  • Correlation: any two contacts that look related across monitors, and anything that looks related to an earlier entry.
  • COMM: any call from outside OER, and any call that was supposed to come and did not.
  • Relief: anything you see while covering. Covering a seat means doing that seat's escalation.

OPS DUTY

OPS DUTY is the off-shift Watch Lead on the duty roster, one week at a time, posted at the Lead position. OPS DUTY can authorize overtime, call people in, open the phone bridge for a long event, and ask the Technical Lead for a Site B switchover. OPS DUTY does not take the watch over the phone; the Lead on the floor keeps it.

If OPS DUTY does not answer in 10 minutes, call the other Leads of the same crew, then the Technical Lead on the engineering ladder (Escalation: Engineering).

Logging

The Lead logs every call made under this page: time, who, answered or not, what was agreed. Type: Communications. A call that was not answered is logged too.

WARNING: A quiet board is reported as quiet only after checking LAST GOOD DATA on each tile. "No new reports" and "nothing happening" are different statements. See Troubleshooting: Feed Silent or Data Old.

Who to call

  1. Guard desk, ext 4020, staffed 24 hours. Anything about a person, a door, a badge, a vehicle or a package.
  2. Security engineer (owner in Escalation: Engineering), through the duty pager after hours, for anything involving accounts, the access system, the machine room or OER data.
  3. Police are called by the guard desk. If people are in danger and the guard desk does not answer at once, call outside emergency services yourself.

The guard desk keeps its own log. The Lead also logs the event in the watch log (type: Administrative Notice) with the guard desk's reference.

articles.title: Emergency Call-Out
articles.summary: Starting the call-out tree when people are needed on site, and reporting back.

revs.s: From the Employee Handbook section on call-out.
Started by OPS DUTY, not the floor.
Call-out may be used to keep people away as well as bring them in.

articles.html:
The call-out reaches every member of staff through the phone tree. It is used when the watch floor needs people who are not on shift, or when everyone must be told something before their next shift.

Who can start it

  • OPS DUTY, or the Lead on the floor if OPS DUTY cannot be reached in 10 minutes.
  • The Technical Lead, for Engineering.

Starting it

  1. Write the message down first, in one or two sentences: what, where to report (or not to report), by when.
  2. The watch floor desk calls the top of each branch of the tree and reads the message.
  3. Each person calls the people listed under them and reads the same message.
  4. If someone cannot be reached in 10 minutes, call the people they would have called.
  5. Home numbers are in the sealed contact file in the security office safe. The guard desk opens it and signs the seal log.

Reporting back

  • When your branch is complete, call back the person who called you: how many reached, who was not.
  • The desk keeps a tally on the call-out sheet in binder 1 and logs the time the last branch reported.
  • Anyone not reached is tried again every 30 minutes until reached or the call-out is closed.
NOTE: The call-out is tested once a year, on a weekday evening, with a message that says it is a test. Results go in the watch log.

Most of our sources are public agencies. They publish their data for everyone and do not take calls about a single user. The card at the watch desk lists, for each source, where its status notices appear and who to contact for a long outage.

Before contacting a provider

  1. Check the provider's own status notice or page.
  2. Check the source from a desk PC, not only from the collector. If it works from the desk PC and not from the collector, it is ours. See Runbook: Feed Outage.
  3. Check whether other sources stopped at the same time. If they did, the cause is probably shared and sits between us and them. See External Service Dependencies.

Each watch has four seats and the crew has one relief. The Lead position faces the wall; the other three seats are in the front console row in the order below. Layout: FLR-002 F.

The wall

  • Left: Event Feed. Centre: Radar. Right and below: Monitoring Grid. The wall mirrors the watch wall console view.
  • Wall clocks: UTC, facility local time, and Site B local time.
  • The wall is not the record. If the wall and a console disagree, the console is right and the wall is a fault for the duty engineer.

Console screens

  • Screen 1: your seat's main view (Grid for Monitoring, Event Log for Correlation, message log for COMM).
  • Screen 2: the watch log entry form.
  • Screen 3: whatever the seat needs. The Lead keeps the turnover sheet open here.

Rules for every seat

  • Never leave a seat empty without telling the Lead. Relief or the Lead sits in while you are away.
  • Badge worn and visible. See Badges.
  • Write your own entries. Nobody signs for someone else. See Writing Watch Log Entries.
  • If you are covering, you do that seat's job, including its escalation. See Escalation: Watch Floor.

articles.title: Shift Turnover
articles.summary: The 06:45 and 18:45 handover: what is read, who signs, and the acceptance row.

revs.s: Handover by phone bridge when distancing is in effect.
Turnover summary service trial from 12 January.
The draft is not the record until signed.
Writing the turnover by hand: what to include.

articles.html:
Turnover is 06:45-07:00 and 18:45-19:00. The oncoming crew is seated by 06:45 / 18:45. The outgoing Lead holds the watch until the oncoming Lead signs the acceptance row.

Order

  1. Outgoing Lead reads the turnover sheet: overall status of each monitor, open items, calls expected, visitors in the building, anything unusual about the floor or the plant.
  2. Each outgoing seat tells its oncoming seat anything specific to it (provider notices for COMM, open correlations, tiles to watch).
  3. Oncoming Lead reads back the open items.
  4. Oncoming Lead writes the acceptance row at 07:00 / 19:00: the seats and who is in them, and any cover. See Leave, Cover and Overtime.
  5. Outgoing crew stays until the acceptance row is in.

Wording

  • A status carried forward from an earlier check is written as carried forward, not as freshly checked.
  • "Clear" is not used to mean that no new report was received.
  • Each open item says the last confirmed observation, the next check due, and the seat that owns it.

Turnover summary service

From 12 January 2026 a summary service drafts the turnover at 06:35 and 18:45 from the shift's log rows. The outgoing Lead reads it, corrects it and signs it. The draft is not the record until it is signed.

NOTE: When the draft is late or wrong, write the turnover by hand. It takes about fifteen minutes. Include every tile that changed level during the shift, every call made or expected, and every open item, in that order. Blue Night has written its own since May and keeps the draft on file only.

When the oncoming Lead is not there

The outgoing Lead holds the watch and calls OPS DUTY (ext 4011). The senior oncoming seat does not take the watch unless OPS DUTY says so. See Escalation: Watch Floor.

articles.title: Writing Watch Log Entries
articles.summary: Entry types, time, wording, and what makes an entry useful to the next shift.

revs.s: Keep the record short; keep it complete.
Name the service at fault, not only the feed (Engineering request).

articles.html:
The watch log is the record of the floor. Somebody will read your entry years from now with nothing else to go on. Write so they can.

Every entry has

  • Time, facility local time, to the minute, when the thing happened (not when you wrote it). On clock-change nights see Clock-Change Nights.
  • Type (table below).
  • What was seen or done, in plain sentences.
  • Follow-up: what happens next and who does it, or "none".
  • Your seat signs it. You write your own; the Lead does not sign for you.
TypeUse for
Status UpdateA monitor or the floor changing state.
ObservationSomething seen that is not a status change.
CorrelationTwo or more things tied together, with the reason.
CommunicationsA call made or received, a bridge, a provider notice.
HandoffSomething handed to another seat, crew or Engineering.
ResolutionThe end of an open item: what fixed it, when.
Routine ReviewScheduled checks.
Training/ProcedureA change to how the floor works. Cite the page or binder section.
Administrative NoticeStaffing, visitors, building, anything else.

Good habits

  • Say what you checked, not only what you concluded. "Checked LAST GOOD DATA: 14:02" beats "feed OK".
  • Name the source and, if known, the service at fault: "content network in front of the feed", not just "feed down".
  • One subject per entry.
  • A correction is a new entry that says what it corrects. Never edit an old entry.
WARNING: Never put a password, a door code, a home number or a person's health in the log.

articles.title: Status Levels
articles.summary: NOMINAL, WATCH, ELEVATED, CRITICAL, DEGRADED and DATA SUSPECT: what each means on a tile and on the Radar.

revs.s: From the monitor design notes, in floor language.
What the floor does at each level.
DATA SUSPECT added after the 7 July stale-data day.

articles.html:
Every monitor has an overall status (its tile) and each contact has its own level. The overall status is not simply the worst contact: each monitor has rules, listed on its own page under Monitors.

LevelTileMeansFloor does
NOMINALgreenData arriving, nothing above the monitor's limits.Normal watch.
WATCHyellowSomething worth watching.Monitoring reports it; Lead logs it.
ELEVATEDorangeSignificant event or several watch items.Lead calls OPS DUTY within 15 min.
CRITICALredSevere event.Lead calls OPS DUTY and pages the duty engineer at once.
DEGRADEDgreyThe monitor cannot read its source.Page the duty engineer within 30 min.
DATA SUSPECTgrey, stripedThe source answers, but its newest record is older than its own interval.Treat as DEGRADED. Check LAST GOOD DATA.

Rules

  • DEGRADED and DATA SUSPECT are not quiet. A monitor that cannot see cannot tell you nothing is happening.
  • A level change in either direction is logged. Falls back to NOMINAL are logged too.
  • Contacts keep their own level. A WATCH tile can carry one ELEVATED contact if the monitor's rules say so.
  • Stay-lit contacts (temperature cities, power grid sectors, transportation) stay on the Radar until the next reading replaces them. A stay-lit contact that has not been replaced on time is a DATA SUSPECT question, not a lasting event.
NOTE: On 7 July 2026 five tiles read NOMINAL with current check times from 10:12 to 16:40 while no new data arrived. The checks reached an outside cache that kept answering. DATA SUSPECT exists because of that day. A NOMINAL tile is not confirmation that data is arriving: see Troubleshooting: Feed Silent or Data Old.

articles.title: Monitoring Grid
articles.summary: Reading the tiles: level, summary line, LAST CHECK, LAST GOOD DATA and SOURCE TIME.

revs.s: Tile order matches the source register.
Power grid tile now reads regional grid data.
Freshness check against each source's interval.

articles.html:
The Monitoring Grid is one tile per monitor, in source-register order. The same tiles are on the watch wall and on each Monitoring console. Each tile opens its monitor's own detail page.

A tile shows

  • Name and level (see Status Levels).
  • Summary line: what the monitor sees now, in a few words.
  • LAST CHECK: when the monitor last asked the source.
  • LAST GOOD DATA: when it last accepted a reading.
  • SOURCE TIME: the time the source put on its newest record.

Reading the times

LAST CHECKLAST GOOD DATAMeans
recentrecentWorking.
recentoldThe source answers but we reject what it sends, or it sends nothing new. Duty engineer.
oldoldThe monitor itself has stopped. Duty engineer at once.

SOURCE TIME is often behind LAST GOOD DATA. Some sources publish an hour or more after the fact (the grid data, the transportation incident reports). Each monitor page says how far behind is normal.

Grey tiles that are normal

  • The legacy dial-up line has no tile; its Radar light is always red. See Legacy Dial-Up Line.
  • Expansion slots on the wall are blank on purpose.
NOTE: Since 8 July 2026 a tile turns DATA SUSPECT when the newest record is older than the source's own interval. Until then, compare LAST GOOD DATA with the wall clock yourself whenever the board looks quiet.

articles.title: Radar Console
articles.summary: Contacts, sectors, the ring, source lights and playback on the Radar.

revs.s: Floor notes: what to look at first.
Stay-lit contacts merge back to back.
GPS contacts on the outer edge are satellites, not places.

articles.html:
The Radar shows every live contact from every monitor on one scope. It is a picture of the board, not a map: positions are by sector and source, not exact places, with a few exceptions noted below.

What is on it

  • Contacts: one blip per contact, coloured by monitor, size by level. Click one for its details.
  • Sectors: eight, in node order N1-N8.
  • The ring: the outline carries space weather and near-Earth object status. A coloured ring is not a contact.
  • Source lights: one per monitor, down the side. Red means that source is not reporting. The dial-up light is always red. See Legacy Dial-Up Line.
  • Contact list: worst first. Hover a row to light its blip.

Exceptions to "not a map"

  • GPS contacts sit on the outer edge. They are satellites, not places.
  • AI incident contacts sit at the provider's headquarters city.
  • Earthquakes, wildfires and volcanoes are placed by their real location within the sector.

Playback

Playback replays the last 24 hours or a chosen day. Use it at turnover to show the oncoming crew what moved, and for correlation. Playback is a copy: it can lag the live view by a few minutes.

NOTE: A contact that should have been replaced and was not (a temperature city still showing last hour's reading) is a sign the monitor has stopped. Check the tile's LAST GOOD DATA. See Troubleshooting: Feed Silent or Data Old.

articles.title: Event Log and Event Feed
articles.summary: What the monitors write, what the watch log is for, and how the two fit together.

revs.s: Correlation uses the Event Log, not the wall.
One row per new or risen contact.

articles.html:
The Event Log is written by the monitors. The watch log is written by people. Both are kept.

What the monitors write

  • One row when a contact first appears.
  • One row when a contact's level rises.
  • One row when a monitor's overall status changes, either way.
  • For some monitors, a note when an event is resolved, updated or corroborated by a second source.

The Event Feed on the wall shows the same rows as they arrive.

What the floor does with it

  • Monitoring reads each new row and reports anything at ELEVATED or above to the Lead.
  • Correlation works from the Event Log, not from the wall: the log keeps the detail rows.
  • The watch log refers to Event Log rows by time and monitor. You do not copy the row; you say what the floor made of it.
NOTE: A monitor that is DEGRADED writes nothing. A gap in the Event Log is not a quiet period unless the tiles were reading during it.

articles.title: Troubleshooting: Feed Silent or Data Old
articles.summary: The board looks too quiet, a tile is grey, or a stay-lit contact did not refresh. Floor checks before paging.

revs.s: LAST GOOD DATA, not LAST CHECK.
Several feeds at once: shared cause.

articles.html:
Use this page when a tile is DEGRADED or DATA SUSPECT, when a tile reads NOMINAL but the board feels too quiet, or when a stay-lit contact on the Radar was not replaced on time.

Floor checks (Monitoring, five minutes at most)

  1. Read the tile's three times. Is LAST GOOD DATA older than the monitor's normal interval? (Each monitor page lists it.)
  2. Look at the other tiles. Has anything else gone grey or quiet in the last 15 minutes?
  3. Open the monitor's detail page. Does it show the same times as the tile?
  4. From a desk PC, open the source's own public page. Does it show newer data than we have?

Then

ResultDo
Only this monitor, source shows newer dataPage the duty engineer (ext 4030) within 30 min. See Runbook: Feed Outage.
Only this monitor, source shows nothing newer eitherLog it as a source delay. Page if it lasts past twice the normal interval.
Two or more monitors within 15 minPage the duty engineer at once; tell the Lead it looks shared.
Monitor detail page and tile disagreePage the duty engineer at once.

While a source is out

  • Log the start time and the last good data time.
  • Every hour, the Lead notes on the turnover sheet which monitors are blind and since when.
  • Do not report "no events" for a blind monitor. Report "no data since".
  • When it comes back, log the recovery and the length of the gap. The gap is not filled in afterwards: what was missed stays missed.
WARNING: A check that answers is not proof that data is arriving. On 7 July 2026 every check passed for six and a half hours while five sources sent nothing new.

articles.title: Troubleshooting: Console or Desk PC Failure
articles.summary: A console freezes, a screen goes dark, or sign-in fails. Moving seats and keeping the watch.

revs.s: Desk PC vendor updates: do not restart during turnover.
Sign-in fails during an outside cloud outage: consoles still work.

articles.html:
First

  1. Move. Every console row has a spare position at the end. Sign in there and carry on. The watch comes first; the broken console can wait.
  2. Tell the Lead which position failed and what you were doing.
  3. Log it (Observation) with the console number from the label on the right-hand screen.

Then

SymptomTryThen
One screen darkCheck the screen's power light and cableDuty engineer in the morning
Console frozenWait two minutes, then hold the power buttonDuty engineer within the shift
Sign-in refused at every positionTry a watch floor console, not a desk PCDuty engineer at once
Watch log entry form will not saveWrite entries on paper (form in binder 1)Duty engineer at once; type them in when it is back
Two or more consoles fail togetherDo not restart anythingDuty engineer at once

Desk PCs vs consoles

Watch floor consoles sign in locally and keep working when outside services fail. Desk PCs, mail and the badge station depend on outside services and may not. During the 6 May 2026 outside cloud outage, desk PC sign-in, mail and the summary service were down for two hours; consoles, the archive and the phones stayed up.

NOTE: Never restart a console during turnover. Desk PC updates that need a restart are pushed between 09:00 and 15:00 on weekdays.

articles.title: Phone Bridge
articles.summary: Opening, running and closing the phone bridge for long events, drills and switchovers.

revs.s: Bridge used for turnover during distancing.

articles.html:
COMM runs the phone bridge. The bridge is opened for Site B switchovers and drills, for any event the Lead expects to last more than an hour at ELEVATED or above, and when OPS DUTY asks.

Opening

  1. Lead tells COMM to open the bridge and why.
  2. COMM opens ext 4050 and logs the time (UTC and local).
  3. COMM calls in: OPS DUTY, the duty engineer, Site B if a switchover is involved, then anyone the Lead names.
  4. Roll call in order: Leads, then consoles in seat order, then Engineering, then others.

Running

  • One speaker at a time. Say your seat or name before you speak.
  • COMM keeps the bridge log sheet: who joined and left, decisions, actions with an owner.
  • Read back every decision.
  • Nothing about security on the bridge. See Escalation: Security.

Closing

  1. Lead asks for open items; COMM reads the action list back.
  2. Lead closes the bridge. COMM logs the time and files the bridge sheet in binder 1.
  3. Open actions go on the turnover sheet.

articles.title: Leave, Cover and Overtime
articles.summary: Who covers an empty seat: relief first, then the other crew on overtime, then a holdover.

revs.s: The overtime rule written down as practised.
Shift day for night rows before 07:00.
September: relief covers. No overtime offered this month.

articles.html:
Leave is requested at least 14 days ahead on the Personnel Office form and posted on the leave sheet. The rotation is posted on the watch schedule.

The rotation

Two crews, Red and Blue. A crew works both the Day Watch (07:00-19:00) and the Night Watch (19:00-07:00) on its days, in a 10-day cycle. Each crew has a relief.

When a seat holder is out

  1. Relief covers the first empty seat of the shift day, in this order: Day Lead, Day Monitoring, Day Correlation, Day COMM, Night Lead, Night Monitoring, Night Correlation, Night COMM.
  2. Any other empty seat: the other crew's holder of that seat, on overtime.
  3. If neither can work: a holdover from the other watch of the same crew, up to 24 hours on the floor in total, with OPS DUTY's approval.

The acceptance row names the cover: "Day Watch COMM covered by Blue Crew overtime (scheduled leave)".

Shift day

Night rows before 07:00 belong to the previous day's shift. A seat that is empty at 03:00 on the 5th is the 4th's Night Watch seat.

Sickness on the day

Call the watch floor desk (ext 4010) at least two hours before your shift. The Lead arranges cover by the same order. If no cover can be found, see Escalation: Watch Floor.

NOTE: 2 September 2026: the relief covers the first empty seat as usual. Overtime is not being offered this month. Seats that cannot be covered are listed in the acceptance row.

articles.title: Clock-Change Nights
articles.summary: Spring forward and fall back on the Night Watch: logging, the extra hour and timesheets.

revs.s: New daylight saving dates from this year.

articles.html:
Clocks go forward at 02:00 on the second Sunday in March and back at 02:00 on the first Sunday in November. Both happen on the Night Watch.

Spring forward

  • 02:00 becomes 03:00. The Night Watch is one hour short.
  • The Lead logs the change at 03:00 new time: "Clocks forward. Log time is daylight time from this entry."
  • Nothing is logged between 02:00 and 03:00; there is no such time.

Fall back

  • 02:00 becomes 01:00. The Night Watch works one extra hour; record it on the timesheet form.
  • The Lead logs the change at the second 01:00: "Clocks back. Log time is standard time from this entry."
  • Entries in the repeated hour carry "(second 01:00)" after the time.

Clocks to check

ClockSets itself?
Wall clock, UTCnever changes
Wall clock, localyes, check at 03:00
Consoles and desk PCsyes
Badge readersyes, check the guard desk display
Break room microwaveno

articles.title: Holidays and Weather Days
articles.summary: The floor is staffed every day. Holidays, snow and ice, and getting in when the roads are bad.

revs.s: Weather days after the February storm.
Cots and food after the February cold.

articles.html:
The watch floor is staffed on every day of the year. Holiday pay applies on the six holidays posted each January. Holiday leave follows the normal 14-day rule.

Weather days

  1. If roads are forecast to be bad, the Lead asks the oncoming crew the evening before whether they can get in.
  2. The outgoing crew is asked who can hold over. Holdovers on weather days follow Leave, Cover and Overtime.
  3. Nobody drives in conditions they think are unsafe. Call the desk instead. Not getting in is not a mark against you.
  4. The guard desk can tell you whether the access road and the north lot are clear.

Staying over

  • Cots and blankets in the supply room, enough for one full crew.
  • Food for two days in the break room cupboard, checked each November.
  • Showers in the locker rooms.
NOTE: If the floor cannot keep three seats filled, call OPS DUTY at once. See Escalation: Watch Floor.

articles.title: Site B Switchover: Watch Floor
articles.summary: The watch floor's steps in a switchover or quarterly drill: who goes, the hand-over, the bridge.

revs.s: Automatic steps: still read them out.

articles.html:
Site B is the alternate operations site. Every quarter the watch switches to Site B and back as a drill. A real switchover follows the same steps. Engineering's steps are on Site B Switchover: Engineering; the procedure drawing is SITE-B-002 F; the room is SITE-B-001 E.

Before a drill

  • The drill date is posted two weeks ahead. The crew on shift that day goes; the other crew covers Site A for the drill only if asked.
  • Travel to Site B takes about 40 minutes. The Site B crew leaves Site A 90 minutes before the planned step 1.
  • Binder 3 at Site B is the copy of record there.

The watch floor's steps

  1. Site A Lead announces the drill on the phone bridge and logs the start (UTC).
  2. Site B crew takes their seats: Lead and all four positions.
  3. Hand-over: Site A Lead reads the open items; Site B Lead repeats them back. Bridge order: Leads, then consoles in seat order.
  4. Engineering confirms all eight nodes are reporting to Site B.
  5. Site B Lead takes the watch and logs the time. Site A consoles to standby.
  6. Switchback: the same hand-over the other way, then the Site A Lead logs taking the watch back.
  7. Site A Lead writes the drill report within 24 hours: times, problems, open items.

TARGET: Site B holds the watch within 30 minutes of step 1.

NOTE: Some engineering steps are automatic since 2024. They are still read out on the bridge and checked off on the sheet.

articles.title: Earthquake Monitor
articles.summary: Magnitude limits, nearness to cities, the eight seismic sectors and what to do with a large quake.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1998 monitor sheet.
Real-time feeds replace the bulletin scraper.
City nearness only raises M2.5 and up.
Contacts stay on the Radar for minutes, by level.
Limits M4 / M5 / M6 (were lower; too many WATCH a day).

articles.html:
Reads the national earthquake reports every 5 minutes and places each quake in one of the eight seismic sectors. Live page: EARTHQUAKE MONITOR.

Levels

LevelQuake
WATCHmagnitude 4.0 and up
ELEVATEDmagnitude 5.0 and up
CRITICALmagnitude 6.0 and up

A quake of M2.5 or more close to a large city is raised one level. Smaller quakes near cities are not raised: there are dozens a day near some of them.

The floor does

  • WATCH: Monitoring reports it, Lead logs it.
  • ELEVATED: Lead calls OPS DUTY. Correlation checks the power grid and network tiles for the same sector over the next hour.
  • CRITICAL: Lead calls OPS DUTY and the duty engineer; COMM checks for a call from the node in that sector. Open the bridge if the node does not report.

Quirks

  • Magnitudes are revised in the first hour. A quake can rise or fall a level. Rises are logged automatically; falls are not, so note them by hand when it matters.
  • A quake offshore or in a neighbouring country may sit in a sector for its nearest region.
  • Swarms (many small quakes in one place) show as one busy area on the Radar. Correlation logs the swarm once, not every quake.

articles.title: Temperature Monitor
articles.summary: Hourly city readings compared with the 1991-2020 normals: deviation limits and why a city goes quiet.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1998 monitor sheet.
City contacts stay lit until the next reading.

articles.html:
Each hour, one reading per city from its weather station, compared with the 1991-2020 climate normal for that city, day and hour. Live page: TEMPERATURE MONITOR.

Levels

LevelDeviation from normal
WATCH10 F or more
ELEVATED15 F or more
CRITICAL20 F or more

Above or below normal both count. Cold readings show in cyan on the tile.

The floor does

  • Log level changes. Correlation compares a large deviation with the power grid sector for the same region: heat and cold move demand.
  • A whole region deviating together is one event; log it once.

Quirks

  • Each city has a primary station and a backup. If both are late the city goes quiet and its contact stays from the last hour. A city still showing the previous hour after 20 minutes past the hour is a Troubleshooting: Feed Silent or Data Old question.
  • Stations report a few minutes after the hour; the monitor picks them up on its next check.

articles.title: Power Grid Monitor
articles.summary: Regional demand against forecast in eight sectors. Why the data is an hour behind and when a sector is suspect.

revs.s: Facility power tile: UPS, generator, utility per node.
Rewritten: the tile now reads regional grid data. Facility power moved to the plant pages.
Overall status holds for two hours after a fall.
Limits scaled to each sector's normal forecast miss.

articles.html:
Reads hourly regional electricity demand and the regional forecast, in eight sectors in node order, about once an hour. Live page: POWER GRID MONITOR.

NOTE: This is the national grid, not our building. Facility power is on Runbook: Utility Power Loss and UPS Alarms and Monthly Generator Test.

Levels

A sector is raised when demand moves away from its forecast by more than its limits. Each sector's limits are at least three, four and six times its normal forecast miss for that hour (WATCH, ELEVATED, CRITICAL), and never below the fixed floor limits. Sectors whose forecasts are often off (the southwest) need a bigger miss to be raised.

The overall status holds for two hours after it falls, so one quiet hour does not end an event.

The floor does

  • WATCH sectors: log, and watch the temperature tile for the same region.
  • ELEVATED or CRITICAL: Lead calls OPS DUTY. Correlation checks the network and severe weather tiles for that sector.

Quirks

  • The data runs one to two hours behind. SOURCE TIME is the grid hour, not the time we read it.
  • A sector marked DATA SUSPECT has a forecast too far from demand to be believable (missing member data). It is not raised; it is logged as suspect.
  • Morning solar ramp in the west can look like a sudden miss for an hour.

articles.title: Space Weather Monitor
articles.summary: Geomagnetic storm scale, radio blackouts and the Radar ring.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1998 monitor sheet.
After the May storm: what the floor checks.

articles.html:
Reads the national space weather scales and the planetary K-index every 15 minutes. Space weather has no contacts: it colours the Radar ring. Live page: SPACE WEATHER MONITOR.

Levels

LevelGeomagnetic storm
WATCHG1 and up
ELEVATEDG3 and up
CRITICALG4 and up

Radio blackouts (R scale) are noted on the page but do not raise the tile by themselves.

The floor does

  • ELEVATED and up: Correlation watches GPS, network and power grid. Strong storms can upset navigation signals, radio paths and long power lines.
  • Tell the duty engineer at G4 and up: the node links and the time sources are checked. See Time Sources.

Quirks

  • The ring shows the worse of space weather and near-Earth objects. Read the ring label to see which.
  • Storm levels are often forecast a day ahead. A forecast is not an event; log it as a forecast.

articles.title: Severe Weather Monitor
articles.summary: Active land warnings: which warning types raise the tile, and how many it takes.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1998 monitor sheet (warnings receiver).
Alert feed replaces the receiver; receiver kept as backup.
Warnings only; watches and advisories left out.
Retuned: tile CRITICAL needs two critical-type warnings.

articles.html:
Reads active weather warnings for land areas every 15 minutes. Warnings only: watches and advisories are not shown. Live page: SEVERE WEATHER MONITOR.

Levels

TileNeeds
CRITICAL2 or more tornado, extreme wind or hurricane warnings
ELEVATED1 of those, or 3 or more other serious warnings
WATCH1-2 serious warnings, or a large number of warnings of any kind

Each warning keeps its own level on the Radar and in the warning log.

The floor does

  • CRITICAL: Lead calls OPS DUTY. COMM checks whether a node or Site B is inside a warning area.
  • If a warning covers this building, the Lead decides on shelter. See Evacuation and Shelter.

Quirks

  • Warnings expire on their own time. A tile can fall a level at the top of the hour when several expire together.
  • Large winter storms produce many warnings at once. Count matters less than type.

articles.title: Wildfire Monitor
articles.summary: Large fires not fully contained: acreage and behaviour limits.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1999 monitor sheet.
Fire behaviour raises a fire's level.

articles.html:
Lists wildfires of 1,000 acres or more that are not fully contained, every 30 minutes. Live page: WILDFIRE MONITOR.

Levels

LevelOne fire
WATCH10,000 uncontained acres, or active fire behaviour
ELEVATED100,000 uncontained acres
CRITICAL500,000 uncontained acres, or extreme fire behaviour

The tile also rises with the number of fires of concern (5 or more = WATCH).

The floor does

  • Correlation checks the power grid and network tiles for the sector of any ELEVATED fire. Fires take down lines and links.
  • Fire season (June-October in the west) runs at WATCH most days. That is normal; log changes, not the steady state.

Quirks

  • Acreage is updated once or twice a day by the fire teams. A fire can jump a level at the morning update.
  • Containment figures go up as well as down.

articles.title: Volcanic Activity Monitor
articles.summary: Volcano alert levels and aviation colour codes. Why the tile sits at WATCH.

revs.s: Typed in from the 2000 monitor sheet.
Three volcanoes at WATCH raise the tile.
WATCH most days is real, not a fault.

articles.html:
Reads the observatories' notices every 30 minutes and lists every volcano above normal. Live page: VOLCANIC ACTIVITY MONITOR.

Levels

WATCH / ORANGEWATCH
WARNING / REDCRITICAL

Tile: WATCH with one volcano at WATCH, ELEVATED with three, CRITICAL with any at WARNING.

The floor does

  • Any change: log it. A volcano at WARNING: Lead calls OPS DUTY; Correlation checks the transportation tile (aviation) for the region.
NOTE: The tile sits at WATCH most of the time because one or two volcanoes are usually at WATCH. That is a real reading.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1999 probe sheet.
Legacy circuits card on the page.
If this monitor and others stop together, the cause is upstream of all of them.

articles.title: GPS / Navigation Monitor
articles.summary: Satellite health from the almanac. Unhealthy satellites sit on the edge of the Radar.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1998 monitor sheet.
Generation and launch year in contact details.
Contacts on the outer edge are satellites, not places.
Interference notices: what to check here.

articles.html:
Reads the published GPS almanac every 3 hours and lists any satellite marked unhealthy. Live page: GPS / NAVIGATION MONITOR.

Levels

  • One unhealthy satellite: WATCH. Two or more: ELEVATED.
  • Fewer than 24 healthy satellites: CRITICAL.
  • Almanac older than 7 days: DEGRADED.

Satellites are taken out for planned maintenance regularly. A single WATCH for a day is normal.

The floor does

  • ELEVATED and up: tell the duty engineer. Our node clocks and some systems take time from GPS. See Time Sources.
  • Interference notices (published areas where receivers may not work) are logged by COMM even when the tile does not move.

Quirks

  • Unhealthy satellites are drawn on the outer edge of the Radar in the satellite's direction. They are not places.

articles.title: AI Incident Monitor
articles.summary: Outages and incidents at the large AI service providers, from their status pages.

revs.s: One of these providers drafts our turnover. Note on the turnover page.

articles.html:
Reads each large AI provider's public status page every 30 minutes. Live page: AI INCIDENT MONITOR.

Levels

Provider statusContact
minor incidentWATCH
major incidentELEVATED
critical incidentCRITICAL

The tile shows the worst provider. If too few status pages answer, the tile is DEGRADED.

The floor does

  • Log level changes.
  • If the provider behind the turnover summary service has an incident, expect late drafts and write the turnover by hand. See Shift Turnover.

Quirks

  • Status pages are written by the providers. They are sometimes late to say anything.
  • Contacts sit at the provider's headquarters city on the Radar.

articles.title: Near-Earth Object Monitor
articles.summary: Close approaches in the next seven days. Size and distance limits. Shown on the Radar ring.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1999 monitor sheet.
Sizes estimated from brightness when no diameter is published.
Ring shows near-Earth status with space weather.

articles.html:
Reads published close-approach tables every 2 hours and lists every object passing within 5 lunar distances (LD) in the next 7 days. No contacts: it colours the Radar ring with space weather. Live page: NEAR-EARTH OBJECT MONITOR.

Levels

LevelObject
WATCH50 m or larger within 1 LD, or any size within 0.1 LD
ELEVATED140 m or larger within 1 LD, or 50 m or larger within 0.25 LD
CRITICAL140 m or larger within 0.25 LD

One lunar distance is the distance to the Moon, about 384,000 km.

The floor does

  • Log level changes. These are known days in advance; the turnover sheet carries them as expected events.
  • Small objects passing very close are found every few weeks. They rarely matter; log them.

articles.title: Legacy Dial-Up Line
articles.summary: The original out-of-band line to the nodes. Its Radar light is always red. That is normal.

revs.s: Page for a line that keeps getting reported.
Still not disconnected. Tested; no carrier.
Tile removed from the Grid; Transportation has the slot. Radar light kept.

articles.html:
The legacy dial-up line is the modem pool and dial-back line from the first build, the original out-of-band path to the nodes. It was replaced by the out-of-band network in January 2004 (Out-of-Band Management Network) and never disconnected.

  • Its Radar source light is always red: DOWN / NO CARRIER. It is the last light in the list.
  • It has had no tile on the Grid since 6 October 2025, when the transportation monitor took its slot.
  • The network page shows it on a fixed LEGACY CIRCUITS card.
  • Nothing depends on it. It stays connected because nobody has signed to disconnect it.
NOTE: You do not need to report it. If you see it change from DOWN, report that.

articles.title: Engineering Duty Rotation
articles.summary: The duty pager, the weekly handover, response times and what the duty engineer owns.

revs.s: Vacant posts: who carries their systems.
From September: no routine schedule. The pager is still carried.

articles.html:
One engineer carries the duty pager (ext 4030) for a week, Monday 09:00 to Monday 09:00. Every engineer is on the rotation. The rotation is posted in the engineering room and at the Lead position.

The duty engineer

  • Answers a page within 15 minutes, by calling the watch floor desk (ext 4010).
  • Can be on site within 60 minutes when needed.
  • Owns the problem until it is fixed or handed to the system owner, and says so on the call.
  • Writes the maintenance log entry for every call-out. See Writing Maintenance Log Entries.
  • May call any system owner at any hour for their system. See Escalation: Engineering.

Handover

Monday 09:00 in the engineering room. Outgoing reads open items; incoming reads them back; the pager changes hands. Open items go on the duty sheet.

Swaps

Swap with anyone on the rotation; both names on the duty sheet and the Lead told before the swap starts. No one carries the pager two weeks running unless they ask to.

Vacant posts

When a post is vacant its systems are carried by the cover engineer listed in Escalation: Engineering. The cover engineer is the system owner for paging purposes.

NOTE: 17 August 2026: from September Engineering does not keep the routine schedule. Work that has to be done will be done. The duty pager is still carried; call it as before.

articles.title: Change Control
articles.summary: Approval, the change window, the rollback copy, the two-person rule and emergency changes.

revs.s: Planned and completed steps recorded separately.
Manual steps listed in every change.

articles.html:
Every change to a production system has an approval, a plan, a rollback and a record. This includes configuration, patches, cabling and anything in the machine room.

Before

  1. Write the change: what, why, systems affected, steps, how you will check it worked, how you will undo it.
  2. Get approval from the system owner and the release engineer. The approval reference goes in the change and in the log.
  3. Save the current configuration or keep the known-good package. No rollback copy, no change.
  4. Book a window. Standard windows: Tuesday and Thursday 09:00-12:00. Nothing during turnover. Nothing on the watch floor without the Lead's agreement on the day.
  5. Tell the Lead at the start of the window what will be touched.

During

  • Two people for any change in the machine room. See Machine Room Entry.
  • Follow the steps. If a step fails, stop. Record the failed step; do not repeat it quietly.
  • Record planned and completed steps separately.

After

  1. Check the result, not the exit code. Compare version strings before and after.
  2. Tell the Lead the work is done and what to watch.
  3. Write the maintenance log entry. See Writing Maintenance Log Entries.

Emergency changes

When something is broken now and the fix cannot wait for approval: the duty engineer may make the smallest change that restores service, with the Technical Lead told before or immediately after. Write it up as a change the same day and get the approval afterwards.

WARNING: An emergency change is for restoring service. It is never for doing planned work sooner.

articles.title: Writing Maintenance Log Entries
articles.summary: System, action type and entry text. One subject per entry. What a good entry records.

revs.s: From the engineering log style sheet.
Compare with the previous period, not only the limit.
Time of restoration and time of full recovery.

articles.html:
The maintenance log is the record of what Engineering did and found. The maintenance log is read by the watch floor, by auditors and by whoever has your job next.

Every entry has

  • Date and your name (the log fills both).
  • System: the system as named in the register (Facility Power, Regional Nodes, Data Archive...).
  • Action: one of the types below.
  • Entry: what was done, what was found, what is left.
ActionUse for
INSPECTIONLooking at something on a schedule.
TESTINGGenerator, UPS, restore, failover and other tests, with results.
REPAIRFixing a fault. Say what the fault was.
CONFIGURATIONA change. Give the approval reference.
INSTALLATION / REMOVALEquipment in or out. Asset numbers.
PLANNINGSteps toward a project or register revision.
ASSESSMENTReviews, counts, findings.
DOCUMENTATIONDrawing and document issues. Give the register number and revision.

Good entries

  • Numbers, not adjectives: "Fuel 91 percent after", not "fuel fine".
  • For a fault: start time, time of restoration and time of full recovery are three different times.
  • For a test: say how you checked it. A backup is checked by restoring it.
  • Name the drawing when a document changes: "NET-001 revised to rev L".
  • One subject per entry. A second subject is a second entry.

articles.title: Runbook: Feed Outage
articles.summary: A monitor is DEGRADED or DATA SUSPECT. Collector, path, provider, or something in between.

revs.s: Check what the receiving side accepted.
Link up is not feed healthy.
Rejected records: job status is not data status.
Shared outages: content networks and caches.
Check the age of the last good result first.

articles.html:
The watch floor pages when a monitor is DEGRADED or DATA SUSPECT for 30 minutes, or at once when two or more go together. Floor checks are on Troubleshooting: Feed Silent or Data Old.

1. How old is the data?

Read LAST GOOD DATA and SOURCE TIME on the monitor page. Compare SOURCE TIME with the source's own public page from a desk PC. Do this first: on 7 July 2026 every check passed while the data was six hours old.

2. Is it one feed or several?

If two or more feeds stopped within 15 minutes of each other, look for what they share before looking at each feed. Check External Service Dependencies for services listed under all of them (content networks, caches, name service, the outside cloud). Several feeds failing together has never yet been several separate faults.

3. Where does it stop?

CheckIf it fails
Source answers from a desk PCProvider problem. Check its notices. See Feed Provider Contacts.
Source answers from the collector hostOur network path. See Runbook: Regional Node Link Down or the firewall logs.
Collector receives a payloadCollector fault. Check its log; restart only after saving it.
Payload parsesFormat change at the source. Keep the sample payload.
Records acceptedRejected records: read the rejection list.
Monitor reads the new recordsMonitor job fault. See the job's script header for what it needs.

4. Fix and record

  • Restart a collector only after saving its log and the last payload.
  • After the fix, watch two full intervals before calling it recovered.
  • Maintenance log: start, last good data, cause, fix, recovery. Name the service at fault, even if it is not ours and not the provider's.
  • Tell the Lead the time data started arriving again. The gap is not filled in.

The register lists each one with what calls it, what happens when it stops, its owner on our side, and its fallback.

In an outage

  1. When two or more things stop together, open SWA-003 and find the services listed under all of them. Start there.
  2. Record the name of the service at fault in the log, not only the feed or system that stopped.
  3. If the service is not in the register, it is a new entry. Tell the owner.

articles.title: Runbook: Regional Node Link Down
articles.summary: A node stops reporting. Alternate path, out-of-band check, carrier ticket, and when to send someone.

revs.s: Alternate path checked before calling it a link fault.
Encrypted links: check the encryptor too.

articles.html:
Owner: Thomas Reed (ext 4246). Drawings: NET-002 L (wide area network), NET-005 C (out-of-band), NET-007 B (link encryption), NODE-001 E (node layout).

The eight regional nodes collect data in their region and send it to Site A. Nodes never run the watch. A node that stops reporting means one region's collectors are blind.

Steps

  1. Confirm from an independent path: is the node reachable on the alternate link? Is it reachable on the out-of-band network (Out-of-Band Management Network)?
  2. If the node is up on another path, it is a link fault. Move the node's traffic to the alternate link and open a carrier ticket.
  3. If the link is up but no data arrives, check the link encryptor at both ends, then the node's collectors (from the out-of-band console).
  4. If the node is down on every path, call the node's site contact (card in binder 2) to look at the power and the room.
  5. If not resolved in 4 hours, plan a visit. See Node Visit Checklist.

Tell the watch floor

Tell the Lead which region is blind and since when. The Lead puts it on the turnover sheet until the node is back.

Record

Path history in the site folder: what failed, which path carried the traffic, carrier ticket number, time back.

NOTE: A public internet outage in the same region does not mean our link is down, and the other way round. See Network / Internet Monitor.

articles.title: Node Visit Checklist
articles.summary: Planned and unplanned visits to the regional nodes: what to take, what to check, what to leave.

revs.s: Site exceptions noted in the folder.
September visits cancelled. All eight nodes reporting on schedule.

articles.html:
Each node is visited twice a year on a schedule, and whenever a fault cannot be fixed remotely. Two people travel for any visit that opens a rack.

Take

  • The node's site folder (binder 2) and the latest INV-002 E inventory page for it.
  • Spares kit for that node (list in the folder): power supplies, a collector board, patch leads, a console cable.
  • Badge, the node key (signed out, see Keys, Safe and Sealed Envelopes), the site contact's number.

Check

  1. Room: temperature, water, smell, door and lock.
  2. Power: utility, UPS on line, battery age, generator or building backup.
  3. Collectors: each one reporting, clock correct (see Time Sources).
  4. Links: main and alternate up, encryptor in service, out-of-band reachable.
  5. Labels match the inventory. Anything that does not is recorded, not fixed on the spot.

Leave

  • Room as found, door locked, key returned on your return.
  • Visit notes in the site folder; maintenance log entry the same day.
  • Tell the Lead when you leave the node and when you are back.

articles.title: Out-of-Band Management Network
articles.summary: The separate path to every node and host console. When to use it and how to sign in.
articles.html:
Drawing: NET-005 C. The out-of-band (OOB) network reaches the console port of every host, switch and node collector by a path that does not use the main network or links. It came into service on 12 January 2004 and replaced the dial-up line, which is still connected (Legacy Dial-Up Line).

Use it when

  • A node or host does not answer on the main network.
  • You need to see a device's console during a restart.
  • The main network itself is the fault.

Rules

  • Sign in with your own account. Shared console accounts are in the sealed envelopes; using one is logged and needs the security engineer told.
  • Do not make configuration changes over OOB except in an emergency change (see Change Control).
  • Every OOB session is recorded. Say in the maintenance log that you used it.

articles.title: Time Sources
articles.summary: Where our clocks get their time, what happens when GPS is disturbed, and which systems have no second source.

revs.s: Node clocks hold on their own oscillators.
Six systems take time from GPS; three without a second source.

articles.html:
Owner: Thomas Reed (ext 4246).

Site A and every node have a time server disciplined by GPS, with its own oscillator to hold time when GPS is lost. Hosts, consoles and badge readers take time from the site's time server.

When GPS is disturbed

(Interference notices, a strong geomagnetic storm, or several unhealthy satellites. See GPS / Navigation Monitor and Space Weather Monitor.)

  1. Check each time server's status: is it still locked, or holding?
  2. A holding server drifts slowly; under 2 ms a day is normal. Log the drift each day it holds.
  3. If a server has been holding more than 3 days, compare it with another site's server over the network.

Systems that take time straight from GPS

NOTE: If the wall's UTC clock and a console disagree by more than a second, trust the console and page the duty engineer.

articles.title: Monthly Generator Test
articles.summary: Generators 1 and 2 alone, then in parallel. Transfer time, fuel and what to record.

revs.s: After the February cold: block heaters checked.
Schedule and contractor numbers in the infrastructure binder.

articles.html:
Drawings: PWR-005 C (generator plant and paralleling switchgear), PWR-001 J (power one-line).

Once a month, a weekday, 10:00, never during turnover. Two people: one at the switchgear, one at the generators.

Steps

  1. Tell the Lead and the guard desk the test is starting.
  2. Generator 1 alone: start, run 30 minutes on load through the transfer switch. Record transfer time.
  3. Back to utility. Generator 2 alone: 30 minutes on load. Record transfer time.
  4. Both generators in parallel: 30 minutes on load.
  5. Back to utility. Cool-down run as the panel sets it.
  6. Record fuel level for each tank after the test.
  7. Tell the Lead and the guard desk the test is over.

Normal results

ItemNormal
Transfer time10 s or less
Load sharing in parallelwithin 10 percent
Fuel after testabove 85 percent; order fuel below 75

If something fails

Stop the test, return to utility, and call the generator contractor (card in binder 2). See Escalation: Facilities and Contractors. A failed generator test means the plant has one generator until it is fixed: tell the Lead and OPS DUTY.

NOTE: 24 September 2026: test done by Brooks. Generator 1 and generator 2 each 30 minutes alone, then 30 minutes in parallel. Transfer 10 s. Fuel 91 and 93 percent after.

articles.title: Runbook: Utility Power Loss and UPS Alarms
articles.summary: The lights flicker, the UPS goes to battery, or a module alarms. What happens on its own and what you do.

revs.s: Modular UPS: one module down is not an outage.

articles.html:
Drawing: PWR-001 J. Owner: Stephanie Walsh (ext 4253).

What happens on its own

  1. Utility fails. The UPS carries the load on battery at once. Nothing on the floor should go dark.
  2. The generators start and come on load within about 10 seconds of the transfer.
  3. When utility has been back and steady for 5 minutes, the transfer switch returns to utility and the generators cool down.

What you do

WhoDoes
LeadLogs the time; checks every console and the wall are up; tells the guard desk.
Duty engineerPaged automatically. Checks that both generators are on load and the UPS is charging.
Duty engineerCalls the power company if utility is not back in 15 minutes (number on the card).

UPS alarms without a power loss

  • One module alarm: the others carry the load. Duty engineer next working day unless a second alarms.
  • Battery alarm: duty engineer the same shift.
  • UPS on bypass: duty engineer at once. On bypass, the load has no battery behind it.
WARNING: If the generators do not come on load and the UPS is on battery, the floor has minutes, not hours. The Lead starts Site B Switchover: Watch Floor steps 1 and 2 at once, and the duty engineer goes to the switchgear.

articles.title: Runbook: Machine Room Temperature Alarm
articles.summary: Cooling unit faults and a rising machine room temperature. Limits and the order to shed load.

revs.s: In-row cooling for the blade rows.
Load-shed order checked with the system owners.

articles.html:
Drawing: MEC-001 E. Owner: Stephanie Walsh (ext 4253).

Checks

  1. Which unit alarmed? Is it running? Filters, water, power to the unit.
  2. Are the aisle doors closed and the floor tiles in place?
  3. Is free-air assist on when it should be (cool weather) or off when it should be (hot, smoky or humid)?

Shedding load

In this order, with the Technical Lead told:

  1. Test and development hosts.
  2. Batch work over the archive.
  3. Accelerator rows (F).
  4. Never: the database hosts, the collectors, the watch floor systems, the network core.
NOTE: Wildfire smoke outside: turn free-air assist off. See Wildfire Monitor.

articles.title: Fire Alarm and Clean-Agent Suppression
articles.summary: What the machine room suppression does, the abort switch, and getting people out.
articles.html:
Drawing: FLR-001 L.

The machine room is protected by a clean-agent gas system. The rest of the building has sprinklers.

When the machine room alarm sounds

  1. First stage (bell): leave the machine room. Everyone. Close the door behind you.
  2. Second stage (horn and strobe): the gas will release after the countdown on the panel. Nobody is in the room.
  3. Call the guard desk (4020) and the Lead. The guard desk calls the fire service.
  4. The duty engineer meets the fire service at the guard desk with the floor plan.

Abort switch

The abort switch by the machine room door holds the countdown while it is held. Use it only if you can see that there is no fire and the alarm is false, and only while someone calls the guard desk. Letting go restarts the countdown.

WARNING: Nobody enters the machine room after a release until the fire service says so. The gas is safe at design levels but the room will be short of air if anything else is burning.

After

  • The fire systems contractor recharges the system. Until then the room has no suppression: the guard desk patrols it every hour.
  • Maintenance log and a security report.

articles.title: Backups and Restore Tests
articles.summary: What is backed up, where the copies are, and the restore test that proves it.

revs.s: Restore from three copies on the anniversary.
Restore test: entry 1. The archive is complete to today.

articles.html:
Owner: Calvin Brooks (ext 4225).

Copies

CopyWhereKept
Live archiveSite Aalways
ReplicaSite Balways
Immutable copySite A and Site B7 years
Tapetape vaultfor ever (see Tape Vault)

The rule

A backup is checked by restoring it, not by the job report. A job that says it succeeded proves only that the job finished.

Monthly restore test

  1. Choose a day. Any day from 15 April 1998 on.
  2. Restore that day's records from one copy (rotate: tape, object store, immutable copy).
  3. Compare record counts and checksums with the manifest.
  4. Record the day chosen, the copy used, the counts and the result.
  5. Once a year, on 15 April, restore the same day from every copy.

If a restore fails

Do not delete or overwrite anything. Restore the same day from another copy. Tell the Technical Lead. Record which copy failed and how.

NOTE: 25 September 2026: restore test, chosen day 12 April 1996, maintenance entry 1. Restored; checksum matches. The archive is complete to today.

articles.title: Tape Vault
articles.summary: The tape vault, the last drive that reads the old cartridges, and the vault keys.

revs.s: Media age tracked in the binder.
Vault keys left at the watch desk.

articles.html:
The tape vault holds every archive tape since 1996. It came into service on 15 November 1999. It is a fire-rated room off the machine room, zone 4.

Rules

  • Two people for any entry. Both sign the vault log.
  • Tapes leave the vault only for a restore test or an off-site exchange, and are signed out and back.
  • Nothing is thrown away. A tape that fails to read is marked and kept.

Drives

The 1996-2016 cartridges need the old drive. It is the last one of its kind on site and is kept powered and tested twice a year with a sample read, oldest first. Do not move it, lend it or replace it without the archive owner.

articles.title: Runbook: Archive Ingest Backlog
articles.summary: Records arriving faster than the archive writes them, or a queue that will not drain.

revs.s: A queue that drains to zero is not a full archive.

articles.html:
Records from the nodes and feeds wait in the ingest queue until the archive has written and indexed them.

Limits

QueueMeansDo
under 10 min of recordsnormalnothing
10-60 minbehindcheck write speed and errors
over 60 minbacklogduty engineer; tell the Lead that the Event Log may lag

Checks

  1. Is the archive writing at all? Look at its last written record time.
  2. Write errors? Disk, object store or index full?
  3. Is the queue growing because more is arriving (a busy event, a node catching up after an outage)? Then it will drain on its own; watch it.
  4. Is one source sending duplicates? Ask the interface owner.

Do not

  • Do not drop the queue to catch up. Every record is kept.
  • Do not restart the archive writer while it is writing; stop it from its own console.
NOTE: 6 May 2026: the archive wrote every record it received. For 2 hours 10 minutes it received nothing from outside, and nothing records what was missed. An empty queue is not a complete archive.

articles.title: Patch Cycle
articles.summary: Monthly patching: test hosts first, Site B before Site A, watch floor consoles last.

revs.s: Watch floor consoles last, by row.
Container images rebuilt, not patched in place.

articles.html:
Owner: Christopher Nguyen (ext 4241). Patches are applied once a month in the change windows (see Change Control). Urgent security patches follow the same order, faster.

Order

  1. Test hosts. Run for two working days.
  2. Site B systems.
  3. Site A support systems (mail, desk PCs, file service).
  4. Site A production hosts, one of each pair at a time. Check the pair before the second.
  5. Watch floor consoles, one row at a time, between 09:00 and 15:00, with the Lead's agreement. Never during turnover.
  6. Node collectors, two nodes at a time.

For every host

  • Version strings recorded before and after.
  • Services checked after the restart, not only the restart itself.
  • A host that will not take a patch is recorded as an exception with an owner and a review date.

Container images

Collectors and feed handlers run as containers. They are rebuilt from the patched base image and redeployed, not patched in place.

articles.title: Accounts: Opening, Closing and Review
articles.summary: New starters, leavers, role changes and the quarterly access review. No owner, no account.

revs.s: Effective permissions checked, not the policy.
Exceptions need an owner and a review date.

articles.html:
Owner: Daniel Price (ext 4257).

New starter

  1. The Personnel Office sends the starter's name, post and start date.
  2. Accounts are opened the working day before the start date: directory account, watch log or maintenance log access by post, mail. Badge from the security office (see Badges).
  3. The starter signs the account form on their first day.

Leaver

  1. Accounts are disabled at the end of the last day, not deleted.
  2. Badge returned at the Lead position or the security office and voided.
  3. Mail held for 90 days, then removed. Files handed to the manager.

Role change

The new access is added and the old access removed on the same day. Never only added.

Quarterly review

  • Every account checked against the Personnel Office list.
  • Effective permissions checked, not the policy that should give them.
  • Accounts not used for 90 days listed; owner asked.
  • No owner, no account.
NOTE: 10 September 2026: access review done. All accounts current. No badges voided; no one has left OER.

articles.title: Site B Switchover: Engineering
articles.summary: Engineering's steps in a switchover and switchback: replication, node transfers, encryptors.

revs.s: Firmware upgrade halted mid-way: never during a drill.

articles.html:
Procedure: SITE-B-002 F. Room: SITE-B-001 E. Power: PWR-002 D. The watch floor's part is Site B Switchover: Watch Floor.

Switchover (A to B)

  1. Confirm replication is current: archive and record store lag under 5 minutes.
  2. Site B: generator started under load, UPS on line.
  3. After the Leads' hand-over: redirect node transfers to Site B ingestion. Confirm all eight nodes reporting.
  4. Check the link encryptors are in service on every node link.

Switchback (B to A)

  1. Replication check Site B to Site A: record counts and checksums match.
  2. After the Leads' hand-over: node transfers back to Site A. Confirm all eight nodes reporting.
  3. Site B to standby; generator cool-down.

Steps 1, 3, 4 and the switchback checks are automatic since 2024. They are still read out on the bridge and checked off on the sheet by a person.

Rules

  • No other change during a drill. No firmware, no patches, no cabling.
  • Drill report within 24 hours in the maintenance log: times, problems, open items.
  • A real switchover outside a drill needs the Technical Lead. See Escalation: Engineering.

articles.title: Restarting a Production Host
articles.summary: Before, during and after a restart: dependants, the console, and checking services one at a time.

revs.s: Check dependants, not just the host.
Outside dependencies marked: 9 of 140 hosts need nothing outside.

articles.html:
Owner: Stephanie Walsh (ext 4253). Host inventory: INV-001 K.

Before

  1. Look the host up in the dependency inventory. List what depends on it, including on the watch floor.
  2. Planned restart: it is a change (Change Control). Unplanned: tell the Lead before, if you can.
  3. Open the host's console on the out-of-band network so you can see it come up (Out-of-Band Management Network).
  4. Save the running configuration and the last log lines.

During

  • Stop services from their own consoles where they have one, in the reverse of their start order.
  • Watch the console through the restart.

After

  1. Host online.
  2. Each dependent service checked one at a time, not only the host.
  3. Scheduled jobs on the host confirmed resumed.
  4. Tell the Lead it is back. Maintenance log entry.
NOTE: The dependency inventory marks hosts that need outside services to start. 131 of 140 do. If an outside service is down, a host that is restarted may not come back until it returns: check External Service Dependencies before restarting during an outside outage.

articles.title: Badges
articles.summary: The OER-5 card and mobile credential, PINs, wearing the badge, and the badge history.

Every member of staff has one OER badge. The current series is OER-5 (issued 12 April 2021): a card and a mobile credential on a phone. Either opens a door; zones 3 and 4 also need your PIN.

Wearing it

  • Remove it when you leave the building. Do not wear it in town.
  • Your photo must look like you. If it no longer does, the security office retakes it.

PIN

  • Three wrong PINs lock the card for 15 minutes. Call the guard desk (4020) if locked out of zone 3 during a shift.

Phone credential

  • The phone must be locked with its own code.
  • A lost phone is a lost badge. See Lost, Stolen or Forgotten Badge.
  • If the phone credential fails, use the card. If both fail, the guard desk lets you in and logs it.

articles.title: Visitors and Guest Badges
articles.summary: Booking a visitor, GC and GN guest badges, escorts, and signing in and out.

revs.s: Escort named in the watch log.
Guest badges re-issued for OER-5 readers.
No new visits booked after 15 August. Booked contractor visits kept.

articles.html:
Booking

A visitor is booked by the member of staff they are visiting, at least one working day ahead, with the guard desk (4020): name, company, purpose, date, areas, escort. Unbooked visitors wait in the lobby until their host comes down.

Guest badges

BadgeForRule
GC-01 to GC-10cleared visitorsunescorted in zone 2; zone 3 only with the Lead (watch floor) or an engineer (engineering room)
GN-01 to GN-10visitors not clearedescorted at all times by a named member of staff

Guest badges never open zone 4. A visitor who must enter the machine room is escorted by two engineers. See Machine Room Entry.

Signing in and out

  1. The guard desk checks photo ID and calls the host.
  2. The visitor signs in at the guard desk and is given a guest badge.
  3. For the watch floor: the visitor is signed in at the Lead position, and the Lead logs the visit with the badge number and the escort's name.
  4. At the end: the badge is returned and logged, at the Lead position and at the guard desk.

Escorts

  • A GN visitor is never left alone. If you must leave, hand them to another named escort and tell the Lead.
  • An escort has one visitor group at a time, no more than four people.
  • A visitor separated from their escort: tell the guard desk at once. See Escalation: Security.

On the watch floor

  • The Lead may refuse or end any visit, at any time, without giving a reason.
  • No photographs on the floor or in zone 4, by anyone, without the Lead's and the security engineer's agreement.
  • Discussion stays inside the published scope of OER monitoring. Questions about anything else go to the designated Engineering contact.
NOTE: 17 August 2026: no new visits are being booked after 15 August. Contractor visits already booked are kept.

articles.title: Lost, Stolen or Forgotten Badge
articles.summary: Report it at once, get a temporary badge, and what happens if it turns up.

revs.s: Badges cancelled in the access system.
Temporary badges need a PIN too.

articles.html:
Lost or stolen

  1. Call the guard desk (4020) as soon as you know, whatever the time. Do not wait to look for it.
  2. The guard desk cancels the badge at once. It will not open any door again.
  3. Collect a temporary badge from the guard desk (photo ID). It works for 7 days.
  4. A new badge from the security office (4021) on the next working day.
  5. If stolen, the security engineer is told and the badge's door history checked.

Forgotten

  • Sign in at the guard desk for a day badge. It opens zones 2 and 3 for your post until 07:00 next morning (19:00 for Night Watch).
  • Forgetting it three times in a quarter is reported to your manager.

If it turns up

Return the old badge to the security office. It stays cancelled. Never use a badge after reporting it lost.

WARNING: A lost phone with the badge credential on it is a lost badge. Report it the same way.

articles.title: Machine Room Entry
articles.summary: Zone 4: who may enter, the entry log, the two-person rule and contractors.
articles.html:
The machine room and the tape vault are zone 4. Floor plan: FLR-001 L.

Who

  • Engineering staff, with card and PIN.
  • Contractors and other visitors only with two engineers present.
  • Watch staff only in an emergency, with an engineer or the guard desk.

Entry log

Sign the paper entry log inside the door every time, in and out, even though the reader records you. The log records why you went in. The security engineer compares the log with the reader record each week.

Two-person rule

  • No change in the machine room with one person present. Change means anything that alters a system: cabling, a card, a configuration at a console, a power switch.
  • Looking, reading a display or fetching a tape (with the vault rules, see Tape Vault) may be done alone, but tell the Lead you are going in and when you are out.
  • Working alone at night: call the Lead when you go in and every 30 minutes. If you miss a call, the Lead sends the guard desk.

In the room

  • No food or drink. No cardboard boxes past the staging area.
  • Floor tiles back in place before you leave.
  • Doors closed. A door held open sets off the alarm after 30 seconds. See Door Alarms and Tailgating.

articles.title: Door Alarms and Tailgating
articles.summary: Door held, door forced, someone following you in. What the alarm means and what you do.

revs.s: Door held and door forced alarms.

articles.html:
One badge, one person

Every person badges at every reader. Holding a door for someone, even someone you know, means the record says only you went in. If someone follows you through a zone 3 or 4 door without badging, ask them to badge. If they will not, or you do not know them, call the guard desk.

You can say: "Sorry, I need you to badge in. It's the rule for this door."

Alarms

AlarmMeansDo
DOOR HELDopen more than 30 s (zone 4) or 60 s (zone 3)close it; the guard desk checks the camera
DOOR FORCEDopened without a badgeguard desk sends an officer; zone 3 or 4 also pages the security engineer
BADGE DENIED (repeated)a badge refused several timesguard desk checks the camera and calls the area

On the watch floor

  • DOOR FORCED on the watch floor door: the Lead looks, does not leave the floor, and calls the guard desk.
  • False alarms are still logged by the guard desk. Do not prop doors to stop them; tell Facilities the door is faulty.

articles.title: Keys, Safe and Sealed Envelopes
articles.summary: Physical keys, the security office safe, the sealed envelopes and the seal log.

revs.s: Plant passwords sealed in the safe.
Tape vault keys at the watch desk.

articles.html:
Keys

Keys are signed out at the guard desk: name, key, time out, time back. Keys are returned the same day unless the security engineer agrees otherwise.

KeyHeldSigned out to
Tape vault (2)guard deskengineering, two people
Node room keys (one per node)guard deskthe engineer travelling
Generator room, switchgearguard deskengineering, contractors with escort
