Supply roomLead positionwatch staff

The safe

The security office safe holds:

  • sealed envelopes with administrator passwords, console accounts and door codes;
  • the sealed contact file (home numbers) for the Emergency Call-Out;
  • the spare guest badges.

Sealed envelopes

  1. An envelope is opened only by the guard desk and the person who needs it, together, and both sign the seal log.
  2. Once opened, the password or code inside is changed the next working day and a new envelope sealed.
  3. The security engineer checks the seal log monthly.
NOTE: 25 September 2026: tape vault keys left at the watch desk, signed for by the Lead.

articles.title: Deliveries and Contractors
articles.summary: Booking a delivery, the loading door, contractors on site and who escorts them.

revs.s: Equipment deliveries to the staging area.

articles.html:
Deliveries

  • Every delivery is booked with the guard desk by the person expecting it: supplier, what, date.
  • Vehicles stop at the vehicle gate. The guard desk checks the booking before the gate opens.
  • Deliveries go to the loading door, then to the staging area outside the machine room. Never straight into the machine room.
  • Unbooked deliveries are refused, politely. The driver may call the person named on the paperwork from the gate phone.
  • Fuel deliveries for the generators: the guard desk calls the duty engineer, who meets the tanker.

Contractors

  • A contractor on site is a visitor. Booked, signed in, guest badge, escort. See Visitors and Guest Badges.
  • Regular plant contractors are cleared (GC badges) for the plant areas only. They are escorted in zone 4 by two engineers.
  • The escort checks the contractor's work order matches what they are doing.
  • Contractor job references go in the maintenance log entry for the work.

Packing material

Cardboard and packing are unpacked in the staging area and removed the same day.

articles.title: Suspicious Packages, Mail and People
articles.summary: Do not touch, move away, call the guard desk. Signs to look for.
articles.html:
A package or letter

Signs: not expected, no return address, too much postage, stains or smells, wires, lopsided, addressed to a title rather than a name, marked "personal" for no reason.

  1. Do not open it, shake it or move it.
  2. Leave the room and close the door. Keep others out.
  3. Call the guard desk (4020) from another room. Do not use a radio or mobile phone within 10 m of it.
  4. Wash your hands if you touched it.
  5. Wait for the guard desk officer and tell them what you saw.

A vehicle

Parked where it should not be, unattended at the gate or by the building: tell the guard desk. Do not approach it.

A person

  • Someone inside without a badge: ask if you can help them, and walk them to the guard desk. If you do not feel safe asking, do not ask: call the guard desk with a description and where they went.
  • Someone outside the fence photographing the building, or asking staff about OER: tell the guard desk. Do not argue or discuss work.

The watch floor

If an item or person means the watch floor may have to be left, see Evacuation and Shelter. The Lead decides; the guard desk advises.

articles.title: Removable Media, Printouts and Clean Desk
articles.summary: Disks, drives and paper: what may leave the building, how it is marked, and how it is destroyed.
articles.html:
Removable media

  • Only OER media, issued by the security office, numbered. No personal drives in any OER computer.
  • Media leaving the building is signed out at the security office. Archive tapes follow the Tape Vault rules.
  • Found media: hand it to the security office. Do not plug it in to see what it is.
  • Failed disks are kept in the security office until destroyed. They never go back to a supplier.

Paper

  • Watch log printouts, turnover sheets and bridge sheets stay in the building. Filed in the binders, or shredded.
  • Shred bins on the watch floor, in the engineering room and in the Personnel Office. The contractor empties them weekly with a guard desk officer present.
  • Nothing from the binders is photocopied for home.

Clean desk

  • At the end of each shift: nothing on the console but the binder and the turnover sheet.
  • Desk PCs locked when you step away. Consoles signed out at turnover.

See also Escalation: Security for reporting lost or missing media.

articles.title: After-Hours Entry and the Vehicle Gate
articles.summary: Coming in outside office hours, the vehicle gate, the lots and the night patrol.
articles.html:
Office hours are 07:30-17:00 Monday to Friday. The watch floor and the guard desk are staffed at all times; everyone else entering outside office hours follows this page.

Coming in

  1. Badge at the vehicle gate. If the gate does not open, use the gate phone to the guard desk.
  2. Park in the north lot. Watch staff park in their seat's numbered space.
  3. Badge in at the lobby. The guard desk officer may ask why you are in.
  4. Engineers called in by the duty pager: tell the Lead when you arrive and when you leave.

The night patrol

A guard desk officer walks the perimeter and the building at 22:00, 01:00 and 04:00, and the machine room once a night from the door. The patrol log is at the guard desk. If you are working somewhere unusual at night, tell the guard desk so the patrol is not surprised.

Walking to your car

After dark, the guard desk will walk you to the lot if you ask. Ask.

articles.title: Camera Recordings
articles.summary: Where the cameras are, how long recordings are kept, and how to ask for one.
articles.html:
Cameras cover the vehicle gate, the lots, the lobby, the loading door, the staging area and the doors of zones 3 and 4. There are no cameras on the watch floor consoles or in the offices.

  • Recordings are kept for 30 days, then overwritten.
  • Only the guard desk and the security engineer view recordings.
  • To ask for a recording (an incident, a damaged car, a door alarm), ask the security engineer within 30 days with the date, time and place. The request and its reason are logged.
  • A recording kept for an incident is copied to numbered media and held in the security office until the incident is closed.

articles.title: Evacuation and Shelter
articles.summary: Fire, threat, severe weather. When the floor is left, who stays, and the hand-over to Site B.

revs.s: The watch floor is never left unattended in a drill.
Real evacuation: hand-over to Site B.

articles.html:
People come first. No console, record or system is worth anyone staying in danger.

Fire alarm in the building

  • In a drill: the watch floor is never left unattended. The Lead and COMM stay at their consoles; everyone else goes to the north lot assembly point.
  • In a real alarm, or if the Lead cannot tell: everyone leaves, the Lead last. The Lead takes the binder and the guest badge list.
  • At the assembly point, the Lead counts the watch; the guard desk counts everyone else from the sign-in sheets.

Leaving the floor for real

  1. Lead calls Site B (4090, or the Site B Lead's number on the card) from the assembly point and asks Site B to take the watch.
  2. OPS DUTY and the duty engineer are told. Engineering starts the node transfers. See Site B Switchover: Engineering.
  3. The Lead logs the time the floor was left and the time Site B took the watch, on paper if necessary.
  4. Nobody goes back in until the guard desk or the fire service says so.

Shelter (tornado warning, threat outside)

  • Tornado warning covering this building: everyone except the Lead and COMM goes to the shelter room (the inner corridor by the Personnel Office). The Lead and COMM go too if the warning says the storm is close.
  • Threat outside: the guard desk locks the building and tells the Lead. Stay inside, away from the lobby windows, until the guard desk gives the all clear.
WARNING: If anyone is hurt, call outside emergency services first, then the guard desk. See Duty Numbers.

articles.title: Transportation Monitor
articles.summary: Airport ground stops, closures and delay programs, and highway, rail and waterway incidents. Type tags and why reports arrive late.

revs.s: New monitor. Takes Grid slot 7 (the dial-up tile's).
Incident reports land one to three hours after the event.
Type tag on every contact: AVIA, RAIL, MARI, SURF.
Two sources; neither is a second source for the other.

articles.html:
Reads national airspace status every few minutes and the national transportation operations center's incident list every 15 minutes. Contacts stay lit until they clear. Live page: TRANSPORTATION MONITOR.

Every contact label starts with its type: AVIA (aviation), RAIL, MARI (maritime and waterways), SURF (roads and bridges). The tile has one colour; read the tag.

Aviation levels

EventCore 30 airportOther airport
Ground stopELEVATEDWATCH
Full closureCRITICALELEVATED
Ground delay programELEVATED from 240 min averageWATCH from 60 min average
DelaysWATCH from 90 minnot shown

Overall: 5 or more ground stops at once = CRITICAL; 4 or more Core 30 airports affected = ELEVATED. Nightly closures and partial runway closures are ignored. The Core 30 are the thirty busiest airports.

Surface, rail and maritime

Each incident type has its own level (closures, crashes with lanes blocked, derailments, bridge and tunnel closures, port and lock closures). Any report naming hazardous materials, a fatality or an evacuation is at least ELEVATED. Incidents stay listed for 12 hours at WATCH and 24 hours at ELEVATED and above, then age out.

Notes in the Event Log

  • RESOLVED: an airport event has ended.
  • UPDATED: details changed without a level change.
  • CORROBORATED: an incident report names an airport that the airspace status already shows.

The floor does

  • CRITICAL: Lead calls OPS DUTY. Correlation checks severe weather, power grid and network for the same sector.
  • An airport ground stop with no weather on the severe weather tile is worth a Correlation entry.

Quirks

  • Incident reports arrive one to three hours after the event, with times in Eastern time. The monitor converts them; SOURCE TIME on this tile is often hours behind. That is normal.
  • Incidents age out quietly; only airport events are marked RESOLVED.
  • The monitor is DEGRADED after 15 minutes without an answer.
  • The two sources cover different things. Neither is a second source for the other.

articles.title: Records and Logs
articles.summary: Every log and record OER keeps: who writes it, where it is, how long it is kept.

revs.s: Paper records listed with the rest.

articles.html:
Nothing on this list is thrown away unless the Kept column says so. Corrections are new entries; old entries are never changed.

On the system

On paper

Links between records

On the records pages (the watch log, the maintenance log, project files, the Document Register, personnel files, the watch schedule and this wiki) a record number in the text is a link to that record:

  • A project code, ENG-yy-nn, opens the project file.
  • A register document number, such as SWA-001 or SITE-B-002, opens its register entry with every revision.
  • An employee number (OER-yyyy-nnn, or NX-10nn for the NEXUS staff) or a full name opens the personnel file. A name two people share is not linked, and neither is a surname on its own.
  • A maintenance entry number, ML and six digits, opens the entry.
  • A nine-digit watch log record number opens the entry in its year's volume.

Links keep the colour of the text and are underlined. To find a record when you only know what it says, use Record Search (Development Host).

Copies

Everything on the system is in the archive and its copies. See Backups and Restore Tests. Paper archived after two years goes to the records room by the Personnel Office, boxed by year.

articles.title: Reading the Watch Log
articles.summary: Finding old watch log entries: by year and day, the text-only version, and how rows are signed.

revs.s: How to find an old entry.
Rows signed from the watch bill.
Searching a year from the development host.
Open a day from the schedule.

articles.html:
The watch log holds every entry since the first watch on 15 April 1998, one volume per year. The text-only version is the same log in plain pages, for printing and for slow screens.

Finding an entry

  • Pick the year, then page through or open a day. Night Watch rows before 07:00 belong to the previous shift day.
  • From the Watch Schedule calendar, any day's bill has a link that opens the log at that day.
  • Every entry has a record number: the year followed by a sequence number. Quote it when you refer to an entry.
  • To find an entry by what it says, search that year's volume from the development host: search -y 2003 outage. See Record Search (Development Host).
  • A record number written in an entry is a link, and so are maintenance entry numbers, project and document codes and full names. See Records and Logs.

How rows are signed

Each row is signed with the name of whoever held that seat at that minute, from the watch bill, the leave sheet and the cover rule (Leave, Cover and Overtime). If a name looks wrong, the watch bill or the leave sheet is wrong: tell the Lead, and the correction is made there, not in the log.

Reading old entries

  • The style has changed over the years. Early entries are short and formal.
  • A status carried forward is written as carried forward. See Shift Turnover.
  • Visitors are never named. Their guest badge number and escort are.

articles.title: Reading the Maintenance Log
articles.summary: Finding old maintenance entries: year volumes, entry numbers since 1996, sorting and opening a record.

revs.s: How to find an old entry.
One volume per year; numbers run on across years.
Search and links. Entry 1 is the first day of the study phase.

articles.html:
The maintenance log holds every Engineering entry since entry 1 on 2 January 1996, the first day of the NEXUS study phase. It is kept in one volume per year. Entry numbers run on from one year to the next and are never reused.

Finding an entry

  • Pick a year, LATEST for the current volume, or ALL.
  • Click any column heading to sort by it; click again to reverse.
  • Click a row to open the full record under it. PRIOR and NEXT step through the log in order.
  • To see every entry that belongs to a piece of work, use its project file. See Engineering Projects.
  • To find entries by what they say, use search on the development host; lookup ML-000042 shows one entry in full. See Record Search (Development Host).
  • Project codes, document numbers, employee numbers, full names and other entry numbers written in a record are links. See Records and Logs.

What the numbers tell you

  • A gap in the numbers is never a deleted entry; there are none. Report one if you find it.
  • Entries are in date order. A late entry is dated when the work was done and says when it was written.

See Writing Maintenance Log Entries for how to write one.

articles.title: System Log
articles.summary: What the systems write about themselves: status changes, failed checks, recoveries, jobs, the hourly summary.

revs.s: New page for the System Log.
A source that answers with old data is logged too.

articles.html:
The System Log is written by the systems, not by people. It is read in Engineering under SYSTEM LOG and covers the last 24 hours, 7, 30 or 90 days. It is never trimmed.

What it records

  • An hourly summary of every monitor.
  • Every monitor status change.
  • The first failed check of a source, by kind only (an error code, a timeout, an unreadable answer), and its recovery.
  • Failed scheduled jobs, by their plain name.
  • Changes in what the public feed accepts.
  • Each month's Radar archive volume when it closes.
  • The temperature day close.
  • Heavy load on the public node: slow-down on and off.
  • A daily traffic line and the nightly backup and health check counts.

What it never records

Error text, addresses, keys or passwords. If a fault needs detail, the detail is in the system's own log and the maintenance log entry.

Using it

  • After a page: read the System Log for the same hour first. It often says which source failed first.
  • A failed check with no recovery line means it is still failing.

articles.title: Document Register
articles.summary: Drawings and documents under control: numbers, revision letters, superseded copies, paper files.

revs.s: Revision letters skip I and O.
Scanned drawings open from the register.

articles.html:
The Document Register lists every controlled drawing and document with every revision since 1996. Engineering owns it. The maintenance log names the revision whenever a document changes.

Numbers

SeriesFor

MECcooling and environmental
PWRpower
NETnetworks
RCKrack elevations, one per row

NODEregional node layout
SITE-Bthe alternate site

Revisions

  • Revision letters run A, B, C... and skip I and O.
  • Every revision stays listed. Superseded revisions are stamped SUPERSEDED; nothing is removed.
  • VIEW opens the drawing. FILE = PAPER means the revision exists only on paper, in the drawing cabinet.
  • Drawings before June 1998 carry the NEXUS // ENGINEERING title block.

Changing a document

  1. The change is approved like any other (Change Control).
  2. The new revision is drawn, checked and signed.
  3. The register entry is added; the old revision is stamped SUPERSEDED.
  4. Maintenance log entry: "NET-001 revised to rev L" and why.

articles.title: Engineering Projects
articles.summary: Project files: what a project is, its window, its outcome, and how log entries join it.

revs.s: Every register revision is a project.

articles.html:
A project is a piece of planned work with a start, an end and an outcome. Almost every project is a register revision or a group of them. The project list is under ENGINEERING // PROJECTS.

A project file shows

  • Its window: planned start and end.
  • Its outcome: COMPLETE, CLOSED (with the reason) or ONGOING.
  • The register documents it changed.
  • Every maintenance log entry that belongs to it, oldest first. OPENED and CLOSED are the first and last of those entries.

How entries join a project

An entry joins a project when it is dated inside the window and either its system matches, its text matches, or it names one of the project's documents. If an entry fits two projects, it goes to the one with the shorter window.

Phases of a major revision

PhaseWhen
PLANabout 12 weeks before the revision date
BUILDabout 6 weeks before
TESTabout 3 weeks before
CUTOVERon the revision date
CLEANUPabout 2 weeks after

Write entries during each phase. A project with no entries in a phase did not do that phase.

articles.title: Watch Schedule
articles.summary: Who is on the floor now, the posted watch bill, and the rotation calendar with each day's bill.

revs.s: Day bill shows leave and cover.
Schedule posted through the end of the year.

articles.html:
The watch schedule is the posted rotation.

  • ON THE FLOOR: today's crew and the watch now, facility time. Before 07:00 it shows the previous day's crew (the shift day).
  • WATCH BILL: every seat and who holds it. A name opens the person's personnel file.
  • ROTATION: a month calendar in crew colours. Click any day for that day's bill: seat holders, anyone on leave and their cover. Future days show SCHEDULED.

The rotation is the 10-day Red / Blue cycle (see Leave, Cover and Overtime). It is posted through 31 December. Swaps are agreed with both Leads and written on the leave sheet; the posted schedule is not changed by hand.

From a day's bill, OPEN THE WATCH LOG FOR THIS DAY goes to that day in the log. See Reading the Watch Log.

articles.title: Personnel Office
articles.summary: Room 112: the directory, organization, photo wall, phone tree, bulletin board, forms and handbook.
articles.html:
The Personnel Office is Room 112, open 08:00-16:30 Monday to Friday, ext 4000.

SectionHolds

ORGANIZATIONthe organization by year.

BULLETIN BOARDnotices posted that year: holidays, clock changes, welcomes and farewells.
FORMSthe forms rack. Leave, timesheets and the rest.
HANDBOOKthe Employee Handbook.

When to go there

  • Leave requests at least 14 days ahead. See Leave, Cover and Overtime.
  • Badge photos are taken here when the security office reissues badges. See Badges.
  • Changes to your name, address or emergency contact. These go in the sealed contact file, never in the wiki or the logs.

articles.title: Network Reference
articles.summary: The posted list of outside networks and services and their last known state. A reference, not a monitor.

revs.s: Typed in from the 1998 COMM card.

articles.html:
NETWORK REFERENCE on the watch floor is the list of outside networks and services COMM kept on a card in 1998, with each one's last known state: ONLINE, OFFLINE, ARCHIVED or UNKNOWN.

  • It is a reference, posted by hand. Nothing checks it.
  • OFFLINE and ARCHIVED services are kept on the list. Nothing is removed.
  • For the state of the internet today, see Network / Internet Monitor.

articles.title: Channel Viewer
articles.summary: The event feed channel and the outside agency channels COMM reads.

revs.s: Event feed published as a channel.

articles.html:
The channel viewer shows OER's own event feed and the public channels of the agencies we read: the earthquake survey, the weather service, the space weather center, the space agency and the cybersecurity standards channel.

  • COMM reads the agency channels for notices that affect a feed (planned outages, format changes) and logs them as Communications.
  • The event feed channel is the Event Log's latest events, published for outside readers. If it stops updating while the Event Log does not, page the duty engineer.
  • A channel that fails to load is shown as such. One agency channel down is not a feed outage; check the monitor's tile.

articles.title: OER ALERTS
articles.summary: Monitor alerts sent to subscribers' phones and computers, and operator notices from the floor.

revs.s: Subscriptions hold only the device and its choices.
One alert per check, listing every new entry.

articles.html:
OER ALERTS sends monitor alerts to subscribers' phones and computers. Subscribers choose the monitors and the lowest level they want for each.

What is sent

  • Every Event Log entry a monitor writes, grouped into one alert per check.
  • A device gets only the entries at or above the level it chose.
  • A device has a daily limit. Past it, alerts are held and shown in its message list, not dropped.
  • Muted devices and quiet hours: alerts are held and shown later, marked as held.

Operator notices

Operator notices are short messages from the watch floor to every subscriber: a planned outage, a known fault, a change to the service.

  1. The Lead drafts the notice: a title and one or two sentences.
  2. OPS DUTY approves it.
  3. It is sent once. URGENT notices reach muted devices too; use URGENT only when people need it now.

Rules

  • Alerts say what the monitor saw. They are not warnings or instructions to the public.
  • A subscription holds only the device's address and its choices. No names.
  • If alerts stop while the Event Log is still being written, page the duty engineer.

articles.title: Public Access Node and Bulletin
articles.summary: The public node (GDK-001), its system use notification, the public log bulletin and how posts are moderated.

revs.s: No links, addresses or phone numbers in posts.

articles.html:
The public access node, GDK-001, is OER's public face: the system use notification, the institutional profile, the public log bulletin, the event records and the monitors. Anyone may connect after accepting the notification. It is separate from the watch floor systems.

The public log bulletin

  • Visitors post a handle (up to 40 characters) and a message (up to 160).
  • Links, email addresses and phone numbers are refused.
  • Text is stored as plain text, never run.
  • SYSTEM lines and automatic replies are posted by the node itself.

Moderation

  • A post is hidden, never deleted. Hidden posts stay in the record with the time and a note.
  • Hide anything that names a private person, gives contact details, threatens anyone, or imitates OER staff.
  • Do not reply to posts as yourself.

Load

The node also carries the Arcade.

When the node is busy it slows its own refresh on the Radar and the watch wall. That is on purpose; the System Log notes it on and off (System Log).

Scores

Moderation

  • A score post is moderated like any bulletin post: hidden, never deleted.
  • Hiding a score post also removes that score from its board, once. Unhiding the post does not put the score back. The moderation note says SCORE DELETED.
  • Hide a score name that names a private person, insults anyone or imitates OER staff.

For staff

  • Not on watch. Not at the console, and not on a watch floor machine.
  • Staff may play from home like anyone else. Staff do not seed, edit or remove scores except through moderation.
  • A cabinet that will not start is an Engineering ticket, low priority. Log it; do not page for it.

articles.title: Record Search (Development Host)
articles.summary: Finding any record from the development host's guest login: search, lookup and open, record numbers and examples.

revs.s: New page. search, lookup and open on the development host.
Wiki pages added to the search.
Watch log: one year at a time.
Examples checked against the current records.

articles.html:
The NEXUS development host still takes a guest login, and from it you can search every OER record published on the network: personnel files and staff profiles, engineering projects, the Document Register, this wiki, the maintenance log and the watch log. Open it from Engineering: DEVELOPMENT HOST. Log in as guest; there is no password. The guest account is read only: nothing typed there changes a record.

Type help to list every command, or help search for one command with examples.

The commands

CommandWhat it does
search <text>lists every record containing the text, section by section
search -y YEAR <text>the same, and that year's watch log as well
lookup <id or name>shows one record in full
open <id or name>leaves the host and opens the record's own page

Searching

  1. Type search and the text: search generator. Put text with spaces in quotes: search "site b". Case does not matter; give at least two characters.
  2. Results come in sections: PERSONNEL, PROJECTS, DOCUMENT REGISTER, OPERATIONS WIKI, MAINTENANCE LOG. Maintenance entries are listed newest first.
  3. Each section shows its first 15 records and says how many more there are. Narrow the search rather than reading them all.
  4. The watch log is searched one year at a time, 1998 to 2026: search -y 1998 orientation adds the 1998 volume. Without -y the watch log is not searched, and the host says so.
  5. Long output stops at --More--: SPACE (or a tap) for the next screen, Q to stop.
  6. Every line starts with the record's number. Use it with lookup or open.

Record numbers

RecordWrite it asExample
Personnel fileemployee number, or full name in quotesOER-2016-001, NX-1001, "Mara Voss"
Maintenance entryML and six digits, or the plain numberML-000001, or 1
Watch log recordthe nine-digit record number199800001
ProjectENG-yy-nnENG-99-03
Register documentthe document numberSWA-001, SITE-B-002
Wiki pagethe page name from its addressbackup-restore

A full name works only when one person on file has it. A surname on its own does not.

Examples

  • lookup ML-000001: the first maintenance entry, 2 January 1996.
  • lookup 199800001: the first watch log entry, 08:00 on 15 April 1998.
  • lookup SWA-001: a register entry with every revision, current one first.
  • lookup OER-2016-001: a personnel file and its staff profile.
  • open ENG-99-03: opens the Year 2000 readiness project file in Engineering.
  • open shift-turnover: opens Shift Turnover here in the wiki.

What it does not search

  • Files on the host itself. Use find for file names and grep for lines in a file.
  • The Event Log and the System Log. Read them on their own pages: Event Log and Event Feed, System Log.
  • Paper records. See Records and Logs.
NOTE: On the records pages the same numbers are links, so a record found here leads to the next one. See Records and Logs.
